paragraphs: The paper studies decision problems with more available choices than there is time to test. In a bandit problem, trying a choice reveals a reward, so learning which choices are good consumes opportunities to benefit from them. When the supply of choices is effectively unlimited, examining every option is impossible.

The authors assume a probabilistic description of how likely a newly selected choice is to have an average reward close to the best possible. They describe this assumption as weaker than those used in earlier work. Their algorithms randomly select a restricted collection of choices and apply upper confidence bounds within that collection, balancing promising rewards against uncertainty.

The analysis gives upper bounds on expected regret, measuring the cost of learning relative to optimal rewards. It also establishes a lower bound that matches the upper bound within logarithmic factors in some cases. That qualified match indicates that, in those cases, substantially better performance is constrained by the problem itself.
neurips-2008-algorithms-for-infinitely-m.tldr: Randomly restricting the choices and using confidence bounds yields regret guarantees for bandit problems with effectively unlimited options.

paragraphs: This paper improves the computation used to perform inference in an existing coalescent clustering model. Its contribution is a sequential Monte Carlo inference scheme: the focus is on how to approximate the model's probabilistic calculations efficiently. The clustering model provides the target, while the new algorithm changes how inference is carried out.

The stated computational improvement is from cubic runtime for the earlier algorithms to quadratic runtime for the proposed method. This changes how quickly computational work grows as the problem becomes larger. The result therefore concerns scalability as well as the time needed for any particular experiment.

The experiments also report better sampling performance than the strongest earlier sequential Monte Carlo method considered. The authors assess this through the variance of estimated likelihood and effective sample size. These findings mean that the computational improvement was accompanied by improvements in those sampling measures in the reported experiments. The evidence supports a useful combination of lower runtime growth and stronger empirical inference quality.
neurips-2008-an-efficient-sequential-mon.tldr: A new coalescent clustering sampler reduces runtime from cubic to quadratic and improves two sampling-quality measures in experiments.

paragraphs: The paper considers resource allocation when jobs arrive one at a time. A job can be completed by spending time on different activities according to a schedule. The central challenge is to learn how to distribute that time while the stream of jobs is still arriving.

The analysis assumes that the fraction of completed jobs is a monotone, submodular function of activity and time pairs. In plain language, the assumption expresses that additional allocations do not reduce completion and that their benefits exhibit diminishing returns. Under this condition, the authors give an online algorithm with near-optimal performance for two objectives: completing jobs before a fixed deadline and reducing average completion time.

They evaluate the algorithm by learning a schedule that divides CPU time among solvers from a SAT solver competition. This connects the abstract activities to concrete computational tools. The contribution is a scheduling framework whose guarantees depend on the stated submodularity assumption and whose practical use is explored through solver allocation.
neurips-2008-an-online-algorithm-for-max.tldr: An online scheduling algorithm achieves conditional near-optimal guarantees by exploiting diminishing returns in resource allocation.

paragraphs: Principal components analysis provides compact representations of real-valued data. The paper addresses the broader problem of dimensionality reduction for data whose statistical behavior is not well described by Gaussian models. Existing extensions, including exponential family PCA and non-negative matrix factorisation, motivate the work but can suffer from overfitting and weak generalisation.

The authors introduce a fully probabilistic PCA approach generalized to the exponential family. Its structure comes from factorising the observed data matrix, connecting a compact representation to a probabilistic model of the observations. Bayesian inference is performed using Hybrid Monte Carlo sampling, making uncertainty part of the inference process rather than relying solely on a fitted factorisation.

The paper presents the model's performance on synthetic and real data. Its central contribution is the combination of exponential family modeling, matrix factorisation, and Bayesian inference within one dimensionality reduction approach. The stated motivation is to address weaknesses of existing methods; the abstract reports demonstrations without asserting a universal improvement over every alternative.
neurips-2008-bayesian-exponential-family.tldr: The paper extends PCA to exponential family data using a probabilistic matrix factorisation and Bayesian sampling.

paragraphs: Simplifying a Markov decision process requires deciding which states can be treated as similar without losing too much information about good decisions. This paper defines a behavioral similarity metric that accounts for similarities between actions as well as states. That makes action matching part of the abstraction process.

The authors prove that states separated by zero distance under the metric form exactly the classes specified by MDP homomorphisms. They also show that the metric bounds differences between states' optimal values. This gives the distance a decision-making interpretation: it controls how different the best achievable values can be. The bound is tighter than the cited bisimulation-based bounds.

The results cover both discrete and continuous action spaces. The paper also supplies an algorithm that uses the metric to group similar states and match actions, constructing approximate homomorphisms. Together, the metric, guarantees, and construction procedure give a theoretical basis for abstraction in an area where previous approaches relied mainly on heuristics.
neurips-2008-bounding-performance-loss-i.tldr: An action-aware state similarity metric supports MDP abstraction and bounds differences in optimal value.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way to construct lower-dimensional representations while seeking to retain meaningful relationships among data points. Its guiding idea is to constrain the transformation to be a diffeomorphism, a smooth, reversible deformation. The authors argue that this is a natural constraint for approximately preserving pairwise distances.

The algorithm first deforms the data so that the points lie near a lower-dimensional subspace, then projects them onto that subspace. These are distinct steps: the smooth deformation arranges the data, and the projection produces the compact representation. This distinction matters because the reversible transformation itself is not the final reduction in dimension.

To find the deformation, the authors reformulate the problem as computing an Eulerian flow field and use ideas from kernel methods to obtain it. They demonstrate the approach on several real-world datasets. The contribution links dimensionality reduction to controlled geometric deformation, with approximate distance preservation serving as its motivation rather than a claim that every distance remains exactly unchanged.
neurips-2008-diffeomorphic-dimensionalit.tldr: The method smoothly deforms data toward a lower-dimensional subspace before projecting it into a compact representation.

paragraphs: Confidence-weighted learning trains a linear classifier online while maintaining uncertainty about its weights. Instead of keeping only one weight vector, it maintains a Gaussian distribution over possible vectors. The covariance describes both uncertainty in individual weights and relationships between them, giving the learning procedure richer information than a single estimate.

The framework imposes confidence constraints: a weight vector drawn from that distribution should classify an example correctly with a specified probability. The paper derives a new convex version of this constraint. It also analyzes the resulting method using mistake bounds, connecting the formulation to theoretical control of errors during online learning.

Experiments on synthetic and text data show lower cumulative errors and lower errors on unseen data than commonly used first-order and second-order online methods. These findings support the new formulation in the evaluated settings. The paper's contribution combines a convex confidence requirement, theoretical analysis, and empirical evidence that tracking uncertainty can translate into effective online classification.
neurips-2008-exact-convex-confidence-wei.tldr: A convex confidence constraint yields an online classifier with mistake-bound analysis and improved errors in synthetic and text experiments.

paragraphs: The paper tackles the computational cost of prediction on large graphs by exploiting the simpler structure of trees. For a weighted tree with n vertices and structural diameter S, it computes a kernel matrix for a selected set of m vertices. The matrix comes from the pseudoinverse of the graph Laplacian.

The stated runtime is O(n + m² + mS). The authors use this calculation for label prediction on a general graph by first replacing the graph with a spanning tree and then applying a kernel perceptron. They consider both minimum spanning trees and shortest path trees as ways to construct that approximation.

Experiments address two web-spam classification tasks, including a graph with 400,000 nodes and more than 10 million edges. Accuracy is reported as competitive with earlier methods that use the full graph. The result suggests that, in these tasks, a tree approximation can retain useful predictive information while enabling efficient computation at a substantial graph scale.
neurips-2008-fast-prediction-on-a-tree-5.tldr: Fast tree-based kernel computation enables large-graph prediction with competitive accuracy in web-spam experiments.

paragraphs: Factor graphs describe probabilistic models in a form suited to message-passing inference. Mixture models create a representational difficulty because their message equations contain nested structure. Ordinary factor graphs do not capture that structure well unless the whole mixture is collapsed into one factor, which obscures its internal organization.

The paper introduces gates as a graphical notation for this containment structure. Gates express mixture models and independence relationships that depend on context. By displaying which parts of the model sit inside which contexts, the notation makes both the model's independences and its message-passing equations easier to visualize together.

The authors also present general equations for expectation propagation and variational message passing with gates. Different variational approximations can be interpreted through different placements of gates in a model. The contribution therefore goes beyond a drawing convention: it connects graphical structure to inference calculations and provides a common way to understand alternative approximations for mixtures.
neurips-2008-gates-c857cd38f9.tldr: Gates extend factor graphs to display mixture structure and support corresponding message-passing equations.

paragraphs: The paper examines how to classify fMRI images when each image contains many voxel measurements but only a small number of training examples is available. This imbalance makes overfitting a serious concern: a model can fit the available examples without learning patterns that reliably distinguish new ones. The study uses images collected in research on stroke recovery.

Its central approach is to fit a separate generative model for each condition. Classification then depends on which model makes an observed image most likely. This gives the models a task beyond directly separating labels: they must describe the image data associated with their respective conditions.

For the classification task studied, logistic regression performs poorly even with either L1 or L2 regularization. The authors report substantially better discrimination using the separate generative models. This finding shows that, in this setting, modeling the data within each condition can provide a more effective basis for classification than the tested logistic regression approaches.

The paper also compares generative and discriminative training of exactly the same models and considers weighted blends of the two training objectives. Holding the models fixed allows the comparison to focus on how they are trained. The abstract reports the advantage over logistic regression but does not state which training blend performs best.
neurips-2008-generative-versus-discrimin.tldr: On a stroke-recovery fMRI classification task, separate generative models for each condition achieve much better discrimination than logistic regression, even with L1 or L2 regularization.

paragraphs: When information passes from person to person, each recipient may reconstruct it from memory before passing it onward. The paper studies this process, called serial reproduction, to understand how memory biases shape what survives transmission. Earlier work with pictures and stories suggested that repeated reconstruction transforms information in ways that reflect those biases.

The authors give a formal analysis using a Bayesian model of reconstruction from memory. This provides a general result characterizing how memory biases affect transmitted information. The approach turns the broad idea that recollection systematically changes a message into a theoretical account with predictions that can be examined experimentally.

They test those predictions in two experiments using simple one-dimensional stimuli. The results supply both theoretical and empirical support for interpreting serial reproduction as a reflection of memory biases. Using simple stimuli connects the mathematical account to a more controlled test of the transmission process, supporting the claim that its transformations contain information about the reconstructive tendencies of memory.
neurips-2008-how-memory-biases-affect-in.tldr: A Bayesian analysis and two experiments support the idea that repeated retelling transforms information according to memory biases.

paragraphs: The paper adapts Kernel Auto-Regressive Moving Average, or KARMA, to infer movement from activity in primary motor cortex. Such decoding is relevant both to brain-machine interfaces and to understanding which aspects of neural activity help predict behavior. The method learns online, updating when feedback about the latest inferred sequence becomes available.

KARMA is recurrent and learns a nonlinear model of output dynamics, so movement prediction incorporates temporal structure. It compares inputs through kernel similarity functions. These functions can be designed to incorporate knowledge about the task, providing a way to connect the learning method with the domain's structure.

The authors first use the method to track a monkey's actual hand movements in a three-dimensional motor task. They then test a closed-loop interface with the monkey's arms restrained, allowing task performance through the interface alone. They compare tracking performance with other leading methods and report interface results. The study therefore examines both movement reconstruction and the use of inferred movement within an active control loop.
neurips-2008-kernel-arma-for-hand-tracki.tldr: An online recurrent kernel method decodes motor-cortex activity for hand tracking and closed-loop brain-machine control.

paragraphs: Image annotation systems assign category labels to regions within images, but obtaining extensive region-level labels is difficult. This paper explores how to learn from partially labeled data. The challenge is to use information in image appearance while also learning the relationship between that appearance and the labels that are available.

The proposed framework combines a generative topic model of image appearance with discriminative label prediction. The topic model represents latent structure in the visual data, while the discriminative component connects the representation to annotation. The authors also develop three alternative ways to impose a spatial smoothness prior, expressing a preference for labels that are spatially consistent.

Tests compare the new models and baseline approaches on two real image datasets. The results support the effectiveness of incorporating latent structure into the annotation model. The contribution is thus a hybrid framework for incomplete supervision, together with alternative treatments of spatial consistency and empirical evidence that hidden structure in image appearance can help label prediction.
neurips-2008-learning-hybrid-models-for-.tldr: Hybrid generative and discriminative models use latent image structure to support region annotation from partially labeled data.

paragraphs: Probabilistic inference in graphical models can involve functions of many variables, making intermediate calculations costly. The paper introduces a multiplicative approximation scheme, MAS, that can be used with different inference algorithms. Its purpose is to simplify those calculations while keeping track of how approximation affects the final answer.

The method uses epsilon-decompositions: a function is replaced by functions involving smaller sets of variables, with a known approximation error. MAS translates these local errors into bounds on the accuracy of the inference result. The authors also study how to optimize the decompositions and give a fast closed-form solution for an L2 approximation.

Applying the scheme to Variable Elimination produces an algorithm called DynaDecomp. The paper reports that it is extremely fast in practice, demonstrates superior accuracy and efficiency, and provides guaranteed error bounds. The central value is the connection between computational simplification and explicit accuracy control: smaller intermediate functions come with a way to assess their effect on the result.
neurips-2008-mas-a-multiplicative-approx.tldr: MAS simplifies graphical-model inference through smaller-function approximations while bounding their effect on final accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper asks when data can reliably reveal the edges of a Gaussian graphical model. It studies an L1-regularized maximum likelihood estimator using independent, identically distributed samples. The setting is high-dimensional: the number of nodes, edges, and maximum connections per node may all grow with the sample size.

The main result gives sufficient conditions for recovering every edge with high probability. Under conditions on the model covariance, the required sample size scales with the square of maximum node degree times the logarithm of the number of nodes. The stated error probability decreases as O(exp(-c log(p))) for a constant c, where p is the number of nodes.

These are conditional recovery guarantees, so the covariance assumptions are part of the result. The scaling also highlights the role of local connectivity alongside total graph size. Simulations show good agreement with the theoretical predictions, supporting the analysis as an account of how this estimator behaves in the studied settings.
neurips-2008-model-selection-in-gaussian.tldr: The paper establishes sufficient conditions for reliable edge recovery by L1-regularized Gaussian graphical-model estimation.

paragraphs: Training visual category models involves choices about how much annotation to request for each image. A simple presence-or-absence label provides different information and requires different effort from a detailed segmentation. The paper introduces a framework that lets the learner choose among these annotation levels as learning proceeds.

The method starts by building a multiple-instance discriminative classifier from the available training data. It then examines unlabeled and weakly labeled examples to decide which annotation to request next. The decision considers both the expected reduction in uncertainty and the relative cost of obtaining the annotation. Each new response is used to update the classifier incrementally.

The key idea is that the best use of human effort may involve a mixture of coarse and detailed labels across images. Treating annotation level as a choice makes that tradeoff explicit. The authors state that this can produce more accurate category models with less total annotation effort, presenting a possibility enabled by strategic allocation rather than an unconditional outcome.
neurips-2008-multi-level-active-predicti.tldr: An active learner selects both images and annotation detail by balancing expected information gain against human effort.

paragraphs: Recognizing handwriting from an image combines two tasks: interpreting visual structure and producing a sequence of text. Many systems handle these separately, extracting image features through specialized preprocessing before passing them to a sequential model. This paper brings the two parts together in a recognizer trained as a whole.

The system combines multidimensional recurrent neural networks with connectionist temporal classification and accepts raw pixels as input. Its design avoids alphabet-specific preprocessing. That matters because the recognition pipeline need not be redesigned around the visual conventions of each alphabet, and the authors present this as enabling use across languages without changing the approach.

Evaluation on data from an international Arabic recognition competition gives 91.4% accuracy, compared with 87.2% for the competition winner. The system outperforms all competition entries on those data. This result provides concrete evidence for the approach's effectiveness and generality, showing that a unified neural recognition system can perform strongly without manually engineered preprocessing specific to the alphabet.
neurips-2008-offline-handwriting-recogni.tldr: A jointly trained neural handwriting recognizer processes raw pixels and exceeds the reported Arabic competition results.

paragraphs: The paper connects two major ways of describing learning in networks. Differential Hebbian learning is based on correlations, whereas temporal difference learning is framed around rewards. These descriptions emphasize different learning signals, raising the question of whether they can nevertheless describe equivalent behavior under an appropriate formulation.

The authors prove an asymptotic equivalence when learning is timed by a local modulatory signal, described in the title as a third factor. Both parts of that statement matter: the equivalence is asymptotic, and it depends on the local signal controlling learning timing. The result therefore establishes a specific mathematical connection between the two learning frameworks.

The authors argue that this connection opens a route to reformulating much of abstract reinforcement learning from a correlation-based perspective closer to neuronal biophysics. That is an opportunity created by the proof, rather than a completed reformulation of the whole framework. Its significance lies in providing a theoretical bridge between reward-centered learning descriptions and more locally expressed mechanisms.
neurips-2008-on-the-asymptotic-equivalen.tldr: A local timing signal makes differential Hebbian and temporal difference learning asymptotically equivalent in the paper's theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: The paper develops sharp bounds on Rademacher and Gaussian complexities for constrained classes of linear predictors. These complexity measures support mathematical analysis of how reliably learning from a sample can carry over to prediction. The aim is to derive several learning guarantees from a shared analysis of the underlying predictor classes.

Consequences include risk bounds under L1 and L2 weight constraints, margin bounds, a proof of the PAC-Bayes theorem, and covering-number bounds. The treatment also includes constraints and margin notions involving relative entropy. Bringing these results together shows how multiple forms of regularization and generalization analysis can be handled through common mathematical tools.

The authors report improvements over several previous risk and margin bounds. They also show that uniform convergence rates for empirical risk minimization closely match online-learning regret bounds for linear prediction, within a factor of two. This connects guarantees about learning from a fixed sample with guarantees about accumulating errors during sequential prediction, while preserving the quantitative distinction between the two settings.
neurips-2008-on-the-complexity-of-linear.tldr: Sharp complexity bounds unify several linear-prediction guarantees and connect statistical convergence rates with online regret bounds.

paragraphs: The paper studies decision-making when the true state is only partially observed and states, observations, and actions are continuous. A particle filter estimates the belief state from past observations, and decisions depend on that estimate. The goal is to improve a parameterized policy by measuring how its performance changes with its parameters.

The authors focus on finite differences, which estimate sensitivity by comparing performance under small parameter changes. They show that a naive implementation suffers from exploding variance. The source is the non-smooth resampling operation inside the particle filter: this internal step makes straightforward sensitivity estimation unstable even though the ultimate target is policy performance.

They propose a more sophisticated finite-difference method that overcomes this problem and prove its consistency. The contribution addresses the interaction between state estimation and policy optimization, rather than treating the particle filter as an inconsequential component. It provides a theoretically supported way to estimate policy sensitivity in the stated continuous, partially observed setting.
neurips-2008-particle-filter-based-polic.tldr: A consistent finite-difference method avoids the variance explosion caused by particle-filter resampling during policy optimization.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning a positive semidefinite matrix while preserving that property throughout learning. Its algorithm, PSDBoost, adapts ideas from boosting and greedy convex optimization to a matrix-valued parameter. The learned object is constrained to have trace one, so maintaining both matrix structure and normalization is central to the formulation.

The key observation is that any trace-one positive semidefinite matrix can be expressed as a convex combination of trace-one rank-one matrices. PSDBoost uses these simpler matrices as its base learners. Building the parameter through such combinations provides a direct structural way to preserve the required properties during the learning process.

This extends the boosting viewpoint beyond combining classifiers: here, the pieces collectively form a constrained matrix. The authors illustrate the algorithm through several machine-learning applications and present numerical experiments. The main contribution is the construction principle and its algorithmic use, showing how a demanding matrix constraint can be respected through the choice of building blocks.
neurips-2008-psdboost-matrix-generation-.tldr: PSDBoost learns trace-one positive semidefinite matrices by combining rank-one matrix base learners.

paragraphs: Matching nearly rigid shapes often relies on distances, because a near-isometric transformation approximately preserves them. Real image data also contain noise and some changes in appearance and scale. The paper argues that these variations can matter even when the shapes are expected to be close to an isometric match.

The authors introduce a graphical model with parameters for appearance, distance, and angle features. They learn all of these parameters through structured prediction, allowing the model to combine several kinds of evidence when choosing a correspondence. The resulting formulation is intended to capture the limited but consequential variations that distance-focused matching can overlook.

Experiments show substantial improvements over recent successful models while keeping running times similar. The reported robustness concerns the scale and appearance variations addressed by the formulation; the setting remains near-rigid shape matching. The contribution is a learned combination of visual and geometric evidence that improves matching in the evaluated cases without a corresponding increase in reported runtime.
neurips-2008-robust-near-isometric-match.tldr: Learning appearance and geometry jointly improves near-rigid shape matching while retaining similar experimental running times.

paragraphs: People often respond faster and more accurately when a stimulus continues a recent pattern, even in randomized experiments where that pattern predicts nothing. The paper asks whether these sequential effects could arise from mechanisms suited to environments whose statistics change. Behavior that looks unhelpful in the experiment may reflect a useful underlying expectation about the world.

A Bayesian model shows that a prior belief in non-stationarity can produce observed sequential effects while the algorithm remains optimal under its assumptions. The authors connect the exact Bayesian computations to an approximate linear-exponential filter, which weights the history through a leaky-integration process. They derive an explicit relationship between the two formulations.

They also show that stochastic gradient descent can tune the leaky process near optimally using only noisy binary inputs. This offers a proof of concept for prediction and parameter learning through standard neuronal dynamics without explicit probability representations. The account explains how such dynamics could be useful and generate the observed effects, rather than proving a unique biological cause.
neurips-2008-sequential-effects-supersti.tldr: Expecting environmental change can make an otherwise Bayesian-optimal predictor exhibit apparently irrational sequential effects.

paragraphs: Predicting an individual animal's learning behavior requires accounting for factors such as stress, motivation, background, and earlier mistakes. Reinforcement learning models can describe behavior, but their predictions depend strongly on settings such as learning rate, exploration versus exploitation, and the discounting of future rewards. Choosing those settings is a central difficulty.

The paper combines a simple reinforcement learning model with an artificial neural network that controls its metaparameters. The network receives inputs including stress, affective phenotype, prior task performance, and neuromodulatory manipulations. This allows the learning model's settings to depend on information about the animal and its experimental circumstances.

The authors report successful prediction of mouse behavior in the hole-box conditioning task. They also describe insights into how stress and anxiety relate to learning, accuracy, and future-reward discounting, and how noradrenergic systems can interact with those processes. The contribution connects contextual and biological inputs to the parameters governing a behavioral model, with demonstrated predictive success in the stated task.
neurips-2008-stress-noradrenaline-and-re.tldr: A neural network sets reinforcement-learning metaparameters from animal and task conditions to predict mouse conditioning behavior.

paragraphs: A robot skill library needs to group similar demonstrated movements and represent each group in a form that can generate behavior. This paper addresses both requirements using human movement trajectories recorded as multidimensional time series. Its organizing principle is similarity in movement dynamics, connecting the grouping process to how a motion unfolds.

The method uses Bayesian mixtures of linear Gaussian state-space models. It automatically determines the number of motion templates by encouraging a parsimonious parameterization. Because inference in the resulting model is intractable, the authors introduce a variational Bayes approximation designed to make efficient inference algorithms usable.

On recorded human Balero movements, the method finds reasonable motion templates and produces a generative model that performs well when executing the task on a simulated anthropomorphic SARCOS arm. The result links learning a library to generating behavior from that library. Its demonstrated execution setting is simulation, and the evidence supports the proposed combination of dynamic clustering, model selection, and motion generation for this task.
neurips-2008-using-bayesian-dynamical-sy.tldr: Bayesian dynamical models cluster human demonstrations into motion templates that support task execution by a simulated robot arm.
